# The kernel card

The whole grammar, on one page. The table below is the kernel, the list of
every word in the grammar. Each word is an **atom**, and the operators join
atoms into a **sentence** that describes a plot. The table is copied from [The
kernel](grammar.qmd#the-kernel) each time the book is built, so it always
matches that chapter. Functions you never write into a sentence, such as
`render_svg()`, are in [Functions around the grammar](utilities.qmd).

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
# The kernel is a table, not a monospace listing, so the rows are emitted as
# markdown rather than wrapped in a code fence, which would print their pipes
# and asterisks at the reader.
#
# The table is the first one in the section, and a sentence may introduce it,
# so its rows are read from the first one to the end of their unbroken run.
g <- readLines("grammar.qmd")
start <- grep("^## The kernel", g)[1]
rest  <- g[(start + 1):length(g)]
rest  <- rest[seq_len(c(grep("^## ", rest) - 1, length(rest))[1])]
first <- which(grepl("^\\|", rest))[1]
rest  <- if (is.na(first)) character() else rest[first:length(rest)]
cat(rest[cumprod(grepl("^\\|", rest)) == 1], sep = "\n")
```

**The minimum sentence** is a source, a mark, and the position channels that
mark needs:

```
data(table) + mark + x(column) + y(column)
```

**The order of `+`** matters in a few places only. Each mark starts a
**layer**: the mark, and the channels and settings that apply to it. In a plot
with one mark, the mark and its channels may be written in any order. This book
usually writes a sentence as *data, mark, positions, refinements*, where the
refinements are the optional parts, such as `color` and `title`. Only two parts
of the order are rules. A sentence must start with a source (`data()` or
`query()`), and a `style()` needs a mark before it. The engine refuses a sentence
that breaks either rule.

What the order does change is which marks each channel or table applies to, and
which mark is drawn on top. A channel written before any mark applies to every
layer that can accept it, and this book writes a channel there when every layer
should use it. A channel such as `color`, written after a mark, belongs to that
mark alone. Positions are the exception: a mark with no `x` or `y` of its own
reads the first ones written. Each later `data()` applies to the mark written
directly after it, and a `style()` styles the nearest mark before it. Two marks
draw in the order you wrote them, so the second sits on top of the first.
[Which orders matter](operators.qmd#which-orders-matter) and [Encoding
scope](encoding-scope.qmd) have the rules in full.

**Deriving** is what `*` does: it joins a transform to a mark, and the mark is
always on the left. More than one transform can follow one mark: `bar * bin *
mean` cuts the `x` axis into bands, then averages `y` inside each band.
Transforms on one mark must each do a different job, and each job is done at
its own step. So the order you write them in does not change the picture, and
writing them in the order they happen is the convention. [Chaining
transforms](transforms.qmd#chaining-transforms) names the four jobs.

**Precedence** decides which operator is applied first. In R and Python, `*`
and `/` come first, then `+`, then `|`. In `data(table) + bar * bin + x(a) |
facet(g)`, the transform joins its mark first. Then `+` joins `data(table)`,
`bar * bin` and `x(a)` into one plot, and the facet splits that plot into panels
last. An atom written after the facet, such as a `title()`, is joined to the
facet first, because `+` comes before `|`. When `|` is applied, the atom joins
the plot, in the same way as an atom written before the facet. So a single plot
needs no parentheses.

Two whole plots joined by `|` or `/` make a **page**, and this book writes each
plot on a page inside its own parentheses. `/` is applied before `+`, so a page
built with `/` is refused without them. Julia gives `+` and `|` the same
precedence, so in Julia a page built with `|` needs them too. JavaScript spells
the operators as words, so it has no precedence to remember.

**When gog refuses**, the message names the rule, and says what to write
instead. **Illegal** means the grammar forbids the sentence you wrote: rewrite
it. **Unsupported** means the grammar allows it and this engine does not draw
it: remove the atom the message names, or use one this engine draws. [Illegal is not the same as
unsupported](design-laws.qmd#illegal-is-not-the-same-as-unsupported) has the
rule, and a refusal of each kind, printed by the engine when the book is built.

**When gog assumes** instead of refusing, the plot still draws. The message is
an **Assumption**: it says what gog decided for you. Read it, and check that the
decision was what you meant.
